analysis.title: Americas Transportation: Eye on Freight: Tracking Trucker Employment; September Adds Inline with Seasonality; October Total Points to Slower
key_insights: Long-haul trucking gained 2,500 drivers in September, in line with the pre-COVID average sequential September increase of ~2,400 drivers. Long-haul data lags total truck employment by one month.
September long-haul adds split into ~1,200 truckload (TL) drivers and ~1,300 less-than-truckload (LTL) drivers month over month.

Total trucking employment (which leads the sub-component data by one month) fell by 1,900 in October, against a typical October gain of 800. GS says this could point to somewhat lower long-haul driver adds in October ahead of peak season.

Adds above seasonality over spring and summer may reflect the improved rate environment. The lower spot rate environment at the end of summer may have kept some drivers on the sideline, and they could return depending on the spot rate path to year-end.
Long-haul driver count in September was ~10% below the 2022 peak and -4.6% versus the pre-COVID peak.

GS expects continued driver supply pressure relative to seasonality, potentially from regulation of non-domiciled CDLs, English language proficiency enforcement and closures of insufficient driver schools. Better rates and wages may draw more drivers in.

Holders of non-domiciled CDLs can drive until their license expires. The newly introduced Dalilah law would limit CDLs to US citizens and permanent residents and require states to revoke non-compliant CDLs, which could have a more immediate effect on driver supply.

Transportation Department actions closed nearly 300 driving schools: 110 had a disproportionate share of CDL applicants who could not pass the English proficiency portion of the test, and 160 had inadequate equipment or space.

Reduced effective truckload capacity from regulatory enforcement is improving TL rates. Rates could rise further if freight demand inflects in late 2026 and into 2027. Dry van truck spot rates were tracking up ~28% YoY excluding fuel in October.
Driver counts remain ~40k below 2019 levels and ~84k below the 2022 peak. GS says it is too early to see capacity returning even as trucking economics improve.

3Q26 earnings from Hunt and Werner showed cost headwinds from driver retention and recruitment. GS attributes this mainly to the Dedicated trucking segment and the lag between paying higher wages and raising rates.
BLS data show long-haul TL wages averaged flat to slightly negative growth in 2025, low-single digits in 1H26, and +5.5% YoY in September.
GS expects contract pricing up into the low double digits to absorb higher wages with room for margin expansion. GS upgraded truckload shares last June.

sector_views.rationale: GS upgraded truckload shares last June on signs of industry stability and better capacity. Tighter driver supply is lifting rates, and contract pricing up into the low double digits should absorb higher wages with room for margin expansion.

earnings_insights: Hunt and Werner 3Q26 earnings prints (already reported) highlighted cost headwinds from driver retention and recruitment. GS sees this as mostly a Dedicated trucking issue, reflecting the lag between paying higher wages and raising rates to cover them.

macro_indicators.reading: +2,500 MoM in September, vs ~2,400 pre-COVID average September add
macro_indicators.interpretation: Adds in line with seasonality, with ~1,200 TL and ~1,300 LTL.

macro_indicators.reading: -1,900 MoM in October, vs typical +800 October gain
macro_indicators.interpretation: Weaker than seasonal. Could point to lower long-haul driver adds in October once sub-component data is published.
Accelerating from flat to slightly negative in 2025 and low-single digits in 1H26, consistent with tighter driver supply.

macro_indicators.indicator: Dry van truck spot rates ex-fuel YoY
macro_indicators.interpretation: Tracking well above last year, consistent with reduced effective truckload capacity.

macro_indicators.reading: up into the low double digit percent range
macro_indicators.interpretation: GS expects this to absorb higher driver wages with room for margin expansion.

risk_factors: Further freight demand weakness could delay the rate recovery.
Wage increases could outrun rate increases, as seen in Dedicated trucking at Hunt and Werner.
Lower spot rates could keep drivers on the sideline, and a spot rate recovery could bring them back and ease the capacity tightness.
Rising wages and better economics could eventually attract more drivers and bring capacity back.

tension_points.bull_case: Regulatory enforcement is shrinking effective truckload capacity, lifting rates. Dry van spot rates are up ~28% YoY and contract pricing is up into the low double digits, enough to absorb wage growth with room for margin expansion.
tension_points.bear_case: Hunt and Werner reported driver retention and recruitment cost headwinds in 3Q26, and long-haul TL wages are up 5.5% YoY. Weak October trucking employment points to slower driver adds.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Freight demand failing to inflect to end 2026 and into 2027, or wage growth outpacing rate increases.

theme_stances.key_argument: Regulatory enforcement is reducing effective truckload capacity and improving TL rates, with contract pricing high enough to absorb wage increases.
theme_stances.evidence: reduced effective capacity in truckload is improving TL rates
